opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and it's one we spend a lot of time on, because "groundedness" turns out to be much harder than it sounds.

The way I think about it is that there's no single switch you can flip. It's really a layered, defense-in-depth approach. The first layer is the system itself: how we retrieve the grounding data and how we instruct the model. We put a lot of work into the metaprompt, essentially telling the model that its job in this mode is to answer based on the provided sources, to cite them, and, importantly, to say "I don't know" or "the sources don't cover that" rather than filling in gaps from its own parametric knowledge. Models really want to be helpful, so if you don't explicitly give them permission to decline, they'll often try to fill in the blank.

But instructions alone aren't enough, so the second layer is measurement. Early on, we had to build ways to actually detect ungrounded content. We developed evaluation approaches, often using a model as a judge, that take the source material and the response, break the response down into claims, and check whether each claim is actually supported by the grounding data. That lets us measure the ungrounded-content rate at scale and see whether a change to the prompt, the retrieval, or the model actually moves the number.

The third layer is mitigation at runtime. Once you can detect ungroundedness, you can do something about it, whether that's flagging it, filtering it, or even having the system go back and rewrite the response so it only includes what the sources support. Some of that work has turned into tools we've made available to customers too, so people building their own applications can check groundedness in their systems.

And then the last piece is the user experience. Citations matter a lot, because they let people verify the answer themselves, and being transparent about what the system is doing helps people calibrate their trust. In a precise mode, users are telling you they care more about accuracy than creativity, so we lean into that tradeoff.

The honest answer is that it's never perfect. It's an ongoing process of measuring, finding the failure cases, red-teaming, and iterating. But having that tight loop between measurement and mitigation is really what's let us make meaningful progress.

r001.rationale: The response describes prompting, evaluation, runtime mitigation, and citations, but does not state that GPT-4’s RLHF post-training penalized answers that departed from the grounding data.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the first thing to say is that "precise mode" isn't a magic switch that makes the model incapable of using its own knowledge. It's really a combination of levers that we tune together, and the goal is to shift the model's behavior so that it treats the grounding data as the source of truth and everything else as context it shouldn't lean on.

The most obvious lever is temperature. In precise mode we run with a much lower temperature, so the model is picking the most likely continuation rather than sampling more creatively. That alone reduces a lot of the drift you see in the more open-ended modes, because a lot of what people experience as hallucination is really the model being pushed toward lower-probability but more interesting-sounding completions.

But temperature is not enough on its own. The bigger piece is the prompting and the orchestration around the model. We're very explicit in the system prompt about what the model is and isn't allowed to do. We tell it, essentially, that the search results or the retrieved documents are the information it should answer from, that it should cite where things come from, and that if the answer isn't in that material it should say it doesn't know rather than fill in the gap. And it turns out models are reasonably good at following that kind of instruction when it's stated clearly and when the retrieved content is actually relevant.

That's the other half, which people sometimes miss: the quality of the grounding matters enormously. If the retrieval step brings back content that doesn't actually answer the question, you've put the model in a position where it either has to say "I don't know" or make something up, and that's a much harder position than if the right passages are sitting right there. So we spend a lot of effort on making sure the retrieval is good, and on things like how much context we pass in and how it's formatted, because that changes how the model attends to it.

And then the last piece is measurement. We have evaluation sets specifically for groundedness, where we check whether the claims in the response are actually supported by the retrieved content, and we also have classifiers running at serving time that look for the model asserting things that aren't in the sources. That lets us catch the cases where the prompting and the temperature aren't enough, and it gives us a feedback loop so that when we change something we can actually see whether groundedness went up or down rather than guessing.

So I'd summarize it as: lower the temperature, be very explicit in the instructions, make the retrieval as good as you can, and then measure relentlessly. None of those by itself gets you there, but together they get you to a place where precise mode really does stay close to the data most of the time.

r001.rationale: The response discusses temperature, prompting, retrieval quality, and groundedness evaluation, but does not state that GPT-4’s RLHF post-training penalized answers that departed from the grounding data.

astra-6.text:
The key is to make the grounding data the boundary of the answer. You instruct the model to answer from the information provided, and if that information doesn’t support an answer, to say so rather than fill in the gaps from its general knowledge.

But an instruction alone isn’t a guarantee. You need to test cases where the answer is in the grounding data, where it’s missing, and where the data only supports part of an answer. The question is whether each claim is supported—not just whether the response sounds right. That also means being comfortable with the model saying, “I don’t have enough information to answer that.”

r001.rationale: The response recommends constraining answers to grounding data and testing support, but does not state that GPT-4’s RLHF post-training penalized answers that departed from that data.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is that grounding is a behavior you have to build and test explicitly. Giving the model a set of documents doesn’t automatically mean it will answer only from those documents. It can still draw on what it learned during training or fill in something that sounds plausible.

So you want to be very clear that its job is to answer from the supplied information, and that if the information isn’t there, it should say so. Then you evaluate that behavior: Is the answer supported by the grounding data? Do the citations actually support the claims? What happens when the question asks for something the sources don’t contain?

That last case is especially important for precise mode. A successful response can be, “I don’t have enough information to answer that.” You have to make that an acceptable outcome rather than pushing the model to always produce an answer.

r001.rationale: The response discusses explicitly instructing and evaluating grounded answers, but does not state that GPT-4’s RLHF post-training for Copilot precise mode penalized answers that departed from the supplied grounding data.
